bull.b: AVLAYAH provides clinical and regulatory proof that Denali’s transport vehicle platform can deliver a CNS-penetrant biologic through approval. This validation may support development of additional programs across lysosomal and neurodegenerative diseases, creating durable platform leverage beyond one product.

Broad early payer coverage reduces a major commercialization barrier for a newly launched rare-disease therapy and supports physician and patient access. The coverage footprint, combined with initial revenue guidance, gives Denali a foundation for expanding adoption as launch execution improves.

Substantial liquidity and low leverage provide Denali with meaningful flexibility to fund clinical development, commercial execution, and additional pipeline investment without immediate dependence on debt financing. This strengthens resilience while the company builds recurring product and partnership economics.

bear.b: Large ongoing operating and free-cash-flow outflows indicate that Denali remains dependent on its cash resources and future financing or partnership proceeds while expanding its business. Continued burn can reduce financial flexibility over time, even with the current strong liquidity position.

The wide gap between current revenue and operating losses shows that Denali has not yet established durable earnings power. Profitability remains dependent on successful commercialization, milestones, or partnerships, leaving results vulnerable to development spending and uneven collaboration revenue.

Delayed or distant clinical readouts extend the period before investors can assess important pipeline programs and may slow evidence of platform productivity. At the same time, incumbent therapies, rival programs, and gene therapies could pressure future differentiation, coverage, and adoption.
